title: A writ petition under Art 32 (Supreme Court) or Art 226 (High Court) seeks enforcement of Fundamental Rights (and under Art 226, other legal rights)

content.overview: A writ petition asks a constitutional court for a writ. Article 32 is the Supreme Court's power to enforce fundamental rights. Article 226 is the High Court's power to issue directions, orders or writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. The usual named writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. The format states the forum, the right or legal duty, the authority's act or omission, why that court has territorial jurisdiction, the grounds, the absence or inadequacy of an alternative remedy where that objection arises, and a specific prayer. Article 32 is not the High Court article. Article 226 is not confined to fundamental rights.
content.short: A writ petition under Art 32 (Supreme Court) or Art 226 (High Court) seeks enforcement of Fundamental Rights (and under Art 226, other legal rights). Exam awareness focuses on parties, grounds, prayer, and the five writs — not a full drafting course.
content.detailed:
Typical skeleton (exam / drafting awareness)

1. Cause title
   • Court name (Supreme Court of India / High Court of …)
   • Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) No. … of …
   • Petitioner(s) vs Respondent(s)

2. Memo of parties
   • Full names, addresses, capacity

3. Synopsis / list of dates (often required in practice)

4. Facts
   • Chronological narrative of relevant facts
   • How the petitioner is aggrieved

5. Grounds
   • Legal grounds (violation of FR / legal right)
   • Cite articles/sections and key cases where relevant

6. Prayer
   • Specific writ(s) sought: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto
   • Interim relief if any
   • Costs

7. Affidavit / verification

Five writs (quick recall)
• Habeas corpus — produce the person; challenge illegal detention
• Mandamus — command a public authority to perform a duty
• Prohibition — stop a lower court/tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction
• Certiorari — quash an order of a lower court/tribunal
• Quo warranto — challenge authority to hold a public office

Art 32 vs Art 226
• Art 32 — Fundamental Right; only FR enforcement; SC
• Art 226 — wider (FR + other legal rights); HC; discretionary

Exam tip: AIBE rarely asks full drafting; it tests which writ fits a fact pattern and Art 32/226 differences.

enhancement.definition: A writ petition is an Article 32 or Article 226 pleading seeking a named writ or direction against a public authority.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The article chooses the court and the class of rights. The writ chooses the relief. A writ petition is not a civil plaint and not a PIL unless public injury and locus are pleaded.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Constitution of India, Articles 32 and 226. The five writs are the remedies those articles authorise. Alternate-remedy practice is case-law and is flagged, not adopted as a holding.
essentialIngredients: Impugned order or omission, with date
Interim prayer only if facts support it
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Article 32 lies in the Supreme Court and is confined to fundamental rights. Article 226 lies in the High Court and extends to fundamental rights and other purposes, so a statutory duty can support a High Court writ even without a Part III plea. The prayer should name the writ. Habeas corpus produces the person. Mandamus commands performance of a public duty. Prohibition stops proceedings. Certiorari quashes a record. Quo warranto tests the title to a public office. The facts must show the authority's act and the petitioner's right. Territorial jurisdiction is pleaded through the seat of the authority or the place of the cause. An alternative-remedy objection is answered with facts if an adequate remedy exists; this note does not state that the objection is always fatal. A private contract dispute against a private person is outside both articles unless a public-law element is pleaded.
examples: Detention without production is an Article 226 habeas corpus petition, with the jailor as respondent.
A licensing authority refuses to decide a statutory application. The prayer is mandamus under Article 226.
A claimant uses Article 32 to recover a contractual price from a private buyer. Neither the article nor the writ fits.
enhancement.problemApplication: Select the article from the right and the court, then select the writ from the relief. Check that the respondent is a public authority and that the impugned act is annexed.
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Drafting notes follow the statutory instrument. Authority for slogans such as bail being the rule remains on the case-law gate.
enhancement.shortAnswerStructure: Article 32 for a fundamental right in the Supreme Court; Article 226 in the High Court for fundamental and other legal rights; name the writ.

keyTakeaways: Article 32 enforces fundamental rights in the Supreme Court.
Article 226 also covers other purposes in the High Court.
The prayer should name the writ.
The respondent is the authority whose act is challenged.
A private money claim is not a writ.

verification.note: Articles and writ names only. No case ratio on alternative remedy added.

content.study: Name the writ that matches the relief. Habeas corpus is custody. Mandamus is a public duty refused. Certiorari and prohibition are directed at jurisdictional error of a body. Quo warranto asks by what authority a public office is held. Do not use Article 32 for a non-fundamental-right State dispute.
